content:
The highly anticipated Beats 360 headphones are officially on sale. After being teased ahead of the World Cup, Apple's latest Beats headphones have finally arrived. I got my hands on a pair early and found them to be a pretty interesting product that's a joy to use — though there is one significant drawback: no wired connectivity, which may be a dealbreaker for some.

Product overview

First, the price: the Beats 360 retails for $349.99. That positions it in the premium market, but still well below the $549 AirPods Max. Coinciding with this launch, the existing Beats Studio Pro has been permanently reduced to $299.99. Of course, it's typically much cheaper at retailers: you can grab one on Amazon right now for about $169.95.

If you've been following Beats' lineup, you'll know that they sometimes use Apple H1 or H2 chips, and other times custom Beats silicon. The Beats 360 uses Beats' own silicon, but with one major upgrade this time: it finally supports automatic device switching via Apple Account, "Hey Siri" functionality, and full Find My integration. If you're someone who loves Apple's products and wants to think of Beats as a budget AirPods Max, the Beats 360 is closer to a true Apple experience than ever before. I was certainly excited to learn this.

Compared to most premium headphones, the Beats 360 is missing one feature: it doesn't auto-pause when you take them off your ears. It takes some getting used to, but you do adjust over time.

Compared to the Beats Studio Pro, the Beats 360 is 12dB louder and has 1.75x better active noise cancellation. They also support Adaptive EQ from iOS 27, and they're the first Beats headphones with an IPX4 sweat and water resistance rating. Both headphones feature Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking, and the Beats 360 gets approximately 8 hours more battery life than the Beats Studio Pro with ANC enabled.

The Beats 360 comes in four colors: Cloud, Sky, Black, and Pink. I personally tried the Sky version, but all four look great.

Custom design

The big selling point of the Beats 360 is the custom design. You can easily swap out ear cushions and headband pads in different colors. There are also two ear cushion options: UltraPlush and Performance Knit. The former is ideal for everyday wear, while the latter is suited for working out.

Each cushion set is priced at $49.99, but there's a launch promotion where a limited quantity is available for just $9.99. For anyone who wants to match their headphones to their outfit or mood, this is a really great deal. I even placed an order for one myself while it's on sale.

The custom design is really the core concept of the Beats 360. With the four base colors and eight additional cushion options, there are 32 possible configurations for the Beats 360. If you mix and match headband and ear cushions freely, that jumps to a whopping 256 different combinations.

You can really make these headphones your own — and it's quite fun to do. Another benefit is that when the ear cushions wear out, you can easily replace them without retiring the entire pair of headphones.

9to5Mac Opinion

For most Apple enthusiasts, the Beats 360 is a solid pair of headphones. If you're transitioning from the AirPods Max and want something lighter and more comfortable, I'd say these fit the bill, but you'll have to sacrifice some sound quality. I also strongly recommend picking up the UltraPlush cushion set, because in my experience, the fabric option gets a little uncomfortable during extended casual wear. Since the cushion set is on sale at launch, there's no reason not to grab one.

I was primarily using AirPods Pro 3 before, but after trying the Beats 360, I found I actually prefer these headphones. The noise cancellation is solid, transparency mode didn't disappoint, and they fold flat, so they don't take up too much room in my everyday backpack. Sure, earbuds are more convenient in many scenarios, but I actually missed these headphones when I left the house (I wasn't allowed to wear them outside during testing), which is something I've never felt about any over-ear headphones before.

Honestly, my only major complaint about the Beats 360 is the lack of wired connectivity. There's no headphone jack, and USB-C doesn't seem to work either. In situations where Bluetooth isn't ideal — like on a plane or connecting to a game console — it can be a bit inconvenient.

Setting that aside, I'm genuinely impressed with what Beats has done with the custom design. These are some of my favorite headphones I've tested in recent years, and they're a step up from the AirPods Max, which have always been uncomfortable due to their weight. The Beats 360 has zero comfort issues as long as you use the UltraPlush cushions.

Pricing and availability

The Beats 360 ships for $349.99, with deliveries and in-store availability starting September 24. You can order through Amazon or Apple.com.

The limited-time $9.99 cushion set deal is available in the US, Canada, UK, France, China, Australia, and South Korea. The promotion runs through October 31 or while supplies last.
